adjective as complement of be etc.

rules.statement: Adjectives have two major uses, attributive modifier in NP structure and predicative complement in clause structure; most adjectives occur in both, and adjectives can also be postpositive (post-head modifier).
rules.condition: Applies to adjective use: attributive = before the noun inside an NP; predicative = complement of a verb such as be; postpositive = after the head noun (something unusual, the money available).

correct.text: an excellent result [attributive]
The result was excellent. [predicative]
something unusual [postpositive]
the money available [postpositive]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: Some adjectives (in some senses) are restricted to attributive function and a few cannot be used attributively, so function must be checked word by word.
rules.condition: Applies to individual adjectives: an attributive-only adjective such as 'sole' cannot be a predicative complement, and an adjective such as 'asleep' cannot be an attributive modifier.
rules.violation: An attributive-only adjective (e.g. sole) is used as predicative complement, or a non-attributive adjective (e.g. asleep) is used before a noun.

exceptions.description: The attributive-only restriction can hold only 'in a given sense' of an adjective, not for every sense; most adjectives occur in both functions.

correct.text: Their sole parent works nights.
The baby was asleep.
an excellent result
The result was excellent.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Lexical restriction: only the words the book names (sole, asleep) are supported here. The full lists need Ch. 6. Do not generalise to other adjectives.

rules.statement: Dependents of adjectives are modifiers (very good, a bit grumpy) or complements (ashamed of him, glad you could come); complements follow the head, so they are hardly permitted in attributive AdjPs but commonly occur in postpositives, and with minor exceptions they are PPs or clauses, not NPs; AdjP has only two levels.
rules.condition: Applies to adjective phrases: modifiers precede the head; complements always follow it and are usually PPs or subordinate clauses; with minor exceptions an adjective takes no NP complement; AdjP and adjective are the only two category levels.

correct.text: It was very good. [modifier]
He seems a bit grumpy. [modifier]
She is ashamed of him. [PP complement]
I'm glad you could come. [clause complement]
the minister responsible for the decision [complement in postpositive AdjP]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Hedges ('hardly permitted', 'minor exceptions') are preserved; do not turn into constraints without Ch. 6.

rules.statement: Unlike adjectives, adverbs do not occur as predicative complement.
rules.condition: Applies to the predicative complement position (as after be): an adjective may fill it, a (-ly) adverb may not.
rules.violation: An adverb (e.g. a form in -ly) is used as predicative complement.

correct.text: Kim was unhappy.
The result was excellent.
She seems quiet.
The answer was clear.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Stated generally on p. 57; Cambridge's treatment of words like 'there' or 'well' in this position is not given here, so exclude them from engine checks until Ch. 6 is processed.

rules.statement: Adverbs generally function as modifiers (or supplements); adjectives modify nominals whereas adverbs modify other categories, including verbs, adjectives, adverbs and NPs, though not every adverb can modify every category.
rules.condition: Applies to modification: nominal heads take adjective modifiers; verbs, adjectives, adverbs and NPs take adverb modifiers; supplements are adverbs detached prosodically from the clause.

correct.text: She almost died. [modifies verb]
an almost empty room [modifies adjective]
He spoke almost silently. [modifies adverb]
They ate almost the whole cake. [modifies NP]
Sadly, the letter arrived late. [supplement]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: 'Not all adverbs can modify heads of all these categories' (p. 57); the engine must not assume 'almost'-style freedom for every adverb.

rules.statement: Adverb is the least homogeneous traditional part of speech; many adverbs are formed from adjectives by adding -ly, and Cambridge reduces the heterogeneity by moving many traditional adverbs into the preposition category.
rules.condition: Applies when classifying adverbs: -ly derivation links many adverbs to adjectives (excellent ~ excellently); the adverb/preposition boundary is redrawn so that words like 'before' and 'afterwards' count as prepositions.

correct.text: excellent ~ excellently
quite excellent ~ quite excellently
a remarkably good performance

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Cambridge narrows the adverb class; Burton-Roberts's boundary not checked.

rules.review_notes: Includes the §6 statement that only a very small number of adverbs license complements (independently of such considerations).

rules.statement: Adverbs can be modified much as adjectives are (quite excellently), only a very small number of adverbs license complements (independently of such considerations), and AdvP has only two category levels.
rules.condition: Applies to adverb phrases: modifiers precede the head; a complement is licensed only by a very small set of adverbs; the levels are AdvP and adverb.

correct.text: quite excellently
independently of such considerations
a remarkably good performance

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: Prepositions are heads of preposition phrases, and words like before, until, afterwards are prepositions whether their complement is an NP, a clause, an adverb phrase, or absent; many traditional adverbs and most traditional subordinating conjunctions are therefore prepositions here.
rules.condition: Applies when classifying words like before, after, until, if, because: if the word heads a phrase with a complement (NP, AdvP, clause) or none, it is a preposition.

correct.text: I saw him before lunch. [NP complement]
I saw him before he left. [clause complement]
I hadn't seen him before. [no complement]
I saw him afterwards. [never takes a complement]
I haven't met him until recently. [AdvP complement]
It depends on how much they cost. [clause complement]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: A major departure from traditional grammar; compare Burton-Roberts's treatment of 'before', 'if', 'because'.

rules.review_notes: Flag for Burton-Roberts comparison: category boundaries differ.

rules.statement: In a PP the NP in 'to you' or 'of the house' is a complement of the preposition, and modifiers like 'a few minutes' or 'straight' before or after the preposition are modifiers; complements may be objects or predicatives (as a liability) and a PP may have no complement.
rules.condition: Applies to PPs: complement = NP object, predicative (after 'as'), AdvP or clause; modifiers precede the preposition phrase; a complement-less PP is allowed (before, afterwards).

correct.text: to you
a few minutes before lunch
They regard him as a liability.
It strikes me as quite reasonable.
I hadn't seen him before.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: The most central prepositions can be stranded, i.e. left with a gap in complement position, when their complement is prenuclear in an interrogative or relative clause; the alternative is to keep the PP together in prenuclear position.
rules.condition: Applies to central prepositions (to, with) in open interrogatives and relative clauses: the PP can be in prenuclear position, or the preposition is stranded with its complement realised by a co-indexed gap.

correct.text: She was talking to a man.
To whom was she talking? [PP prenuclear]
Who was she talking to? [stranded]
the razor-blade with which I cut it [PP prenuclear]
the razor-blade that I cut it with [stranded]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Only the 'most central' prepositions; which ones are not listed here. Do not use as an error rule.

rules.statement: Adjunct covers modifiers in clause (or VP) structure together with the related supplements (e.g. 'Unhappily' in 'Unhappily, the letter arrived too late').
rules.condition: Applies when naming a clause-level dependent that is not a core complement: a modifier in clause or VP structure, or a related supplement detached prosodically from the clause.

correct.text: She left at noon.
Unhappily, the letter arrived too late.
I spoke to her in the garden.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: A manner or locative expression is a complement, not an adjunct, when the verb requires it: 'badly' in 'treated us badly' is obligatory (another sense of treat is involved without it), and locatives with verbs of motion are generally complements, including source and goal.
rules.condition: Applies to manner and place expressions: manner is a complement if obligatory for the verb sense; locatives are adjuncts with static situations but generally complements with verbs of motion; source marks the starting point and goal the endpoint.

correct.text: They treated us badly. [manner complement]
I spoke to her in the garden. [locative adjunct]
Kim drove from Berlin to Bonn. [source and goal complements]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: 'Mostly adjuncts' and 'generally complements' are hedged; Ch. 4/8 hold the tests.

rules.statement: Adjuncts are named on a semantic basis, including temporal location, duration, frequency, degree, purpose, reason, result, concession and condition, plus less familiar concepts.
rules.condition: Applies when labelling adjuncts: choose the label by meaning, using categories such as temporal location, duration, frequency, degree, purpose, reason, result, concession and condition.

correct.text: She left at noon. [temporal location]
They waited for an hour. [duration]
He calls every week. [frequency]
I came to help. [purpose]
If it rains, we'll stay in. [condition]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Only the category names appear in the overview; definitions are in Ch. 8.

rules.concept: not even continuation requires a negative clause
rules.statement: A clause can be continued with 'not even' only if it is negative; a positive clause cannot be so continued.
rules.condition: Applies to clauses followed by a ', not even ...' continuation: the host clause must be negative (clausal negation).
rules.violation: A positive clause (or a clause with only subclausal negation) is followed by a 'not even ...' continuation.

correct.text: He didn't read the report, not even the summary.
They didn't visit the town, not even the museum.
She never wrote, not even a postcard.
We didn't ask anyone, not even Jon.

incorrect.text: *He read the report, not even the summary.
*They visited the town, not even the museum.
*She wrote often, not even a postcard.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: not even continuation requires a negative clause
burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: One of three diagnostic tests; the book describes it as a syntactic distribution difference between negative and positive clauses. 'Never' is treated here as clausal negation by assumption; check Ch. 9 before relying on it.

rules.statement: A negative clause is followed by the connective adjunct nor (or neither) and takes a positive confirmation tag; a positive clause is followed by so and takes a negative tag.
rules.condition: Applies to clausal polarity diagnostics: negative clause + 'and nor did ...' + positive tag (did he?); positive clause + 'and so did ...' + negative tag (didn't he?).

correct.text: He didn't read the report, and nor did his son.
He read the report, and so did his son.
He didn't read it, did he?
He read it, didn't he?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Described as differences in distribution, not as bans on all other combinations.

rules.statement: A clause counts as positive by the three tests even if it contains negative words inside it (subclausal negation, e.g. 'not for the first time', 'in no time', 'unfriendly'); such clauses behave as positive: no 'not even', 'so' rather than 'nor', and negative tags.
rules.condition: Applies to clauses with a negative element inside a constituent: if the clause fails the negative-clause tests, the negation is subclausal; clausal negation passes them.

correct.text: Not for the first time, she found his behaviour offensive.
We'll do it in no time, won't we?
They were rather unfriendly, weren't they?
Not for the first time, she was late, and so was he.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: Negatively oriented polarity-sensitive items (any longer, any, anyone, ever, determinative either, yet, at all, in certain senses) occur in negative and other non-affirmative clauses (interrogatives, if-clauses) but not in positive assertions.
rules.condition: Applies to clauses containing a negatively oriented item such as 'any longer' or 'yet': the clause must be non-affirmative, i.e. negative, interrogative or the complement of conditional 'if', and not a positive assertion.
rules.violation: A negatively oriented item appears in a positive assertion (not negative, interrogative or conditional).

exceptions.description: The orientation holds 'in certain senses at least'; the source does not list which senses are excluded (for example free-choice uses).

correct.text: She doesn't live here any longer.
Will you be needing me any longer?
If he waits any longer, he will miss it.
They haven't replied yet.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Sense-dependent. 'Anyone can do it' (a different sense of any) is outside this record; the exceptions and the full item list are in Ch. 9.

rules.statement: Positively oriented items (somewhat, some, someone, pretty in the degree sense, already, still) favour positive contexts, so 'somewhat' is not acceptable under clausal negation.
rules.condition: Applies to clauses with 'somewhat' (or another positively oriented item) under clausal negation: the item is not acceptable inside a negative clause.
rules.violation: A positively oriented item such as 'somewhat' occurs inside a negative clause.

exceptions.description: The special case where the negative is used to deny or contradict a prior assertion containing the item is set aside by the source.

correct.text: He was feeling somewhat sad.
The soup was somewhat salty.
They look somewhat tired.
The film was somewhat long.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Only 'somewhat' has a starred example. For other positive items (some, already, still) the book says only that they favour positive contexts.

rules.statement: The scope of negation is the part of the sentence the negation applies to; it is not fixed by linear order ('need not' has need inside scope, 'must not' has must outside), and some sentences are ambiguous (a because-adjunct inside or outside the scope of not).
rules.condition: Applies when interpreting negative clauses with quantifiers, modals or adjuncts: an item is inside the scope of the negation if it is part of what is negated; scope can differ from word order.

correct.text: Not many students passed. [many inside scope of not]
Many students did not pass. [many outside scope of not]
You need not answer. [need inside scope]
You must not answer. [must outside scope]
I didn't leave because I was angry. [ambiguous]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.review_notes: Interpretation, not grammaticality. Not for the error-detection engine.

rules.statement: Clause type contrasts declaratives, closed interrogatives, open interrogatives, exclamatives and imperatives, and is a category of syntactic form distinct from meaning or use (a declarative with rising intonation can ask a question).
rules.condition: Applies when classifying clause type by form: declarative, closed interrogative, open interrogative, exclamative, imperative; form categories are kept separate from meaning and use.

correct.text: She is a good player. [declarative]
Is she a good player? [closed interrogative]
How good a player is she? [open interrogative]
What a good player she is! [exclamative]
Play well! [imperative]
You're leaving? [declarative in form; used to ask]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: Questions are classified by their set of possible answers: polar (yes/no), alternative (a choice among stated options) and variable (an answer supplies a value for a variable).
rules.condition: Applies to the semantic classification of questions: polar = yes or no; alternative = answers are the listed alternatives; variable = answer gives a value for the open proposition.

correct.text: Is this yours? [polar]
Is this Kim's or Pat's? [alternative]
Whose is this? [variable]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: Speech acts such as statements, questions and orders have illocutionary force; directive is the force typically associated with imperatives, and many forces go beyond the syntactic categories (e.g. a declarative used as a promise or apology).
rules.condition: Applies when interpreting use rather than form: force is a matter of what the utterance does; a clause type is only typically linked to a force.

correct.text: Play well! [directive]
I promise to be home by six. [declarative used as a promise]
We apologise for the delay. [declarative used as an apology]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

rules.statement: Illocutionary meaning is often conveyed indirectly: a closed interrogative like 'Would you like to close the window?' is syntactically a question but is likely to be used as a polite directive.
rules.condition: Applies when an utterance's literal force differs from its likely use; indirect directives are common and are often considered more polite than direct ones.

correct.text: Would you like to close the window? [closed interrogative used as request]
Close the window. [direct directive]
Could you pass the salt? [closed interrogative used as request]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

conflicts.description: Cambridge moves many traditional adverbs and subordinating conjunctions into the preposition category. Burton-Roberts's boundaries were not supplied and may differ.
conflicts.proposed_resolution: Compare with Burton-Roberts word-class chapters before approval.

uncertain_items.issue: §6 begins at the bottom of printed p. 57, immediately after the §5 count/non-count passage; page boundary is shared with the previous batch.
Words like 'there' and 'well' and their function are not covered, so WCAT-009 (adverbs not predicative) may over-reach.
Full lists of negatively and positively oriented items and the senses in which they apply are not given.
Whether 'never' and similar words give clausal negation (CLS-019) is not stated in §9.
